name: CIRCA original demo content
notes: All artists, shows, people and media in this set are original and fictional, generated for the prototype. Works offline.

creators.name: Juniper Vale
creators.bio: Writes at two in the morning on a secondhand Rhodes she bought from a church sale. Paper Moons is her first release after four years of playing other people's records at a bar on Lexington Avenue.

creators.name: Marlow & the Saltwater
creators.bio: Three friends, two acoustic guitars and a borrowed upright bass. They record in a converted net loft on the harbor, windows open, whatever the weather.

creators.name: Teodora Blue
creators.bio: Synth player, choir kid, former church organist. Builds wide, glowing songs out of analog synths and the reverb of empty rooms.

creators.name: Yemi & the Daybreak
creators.bio: A seven-piece band led by guitarist Yemi Adeyele, playing the highlife records his parents danced to in Lagos, rewired for a Gulf Coast summer.

creators.name: Cass Ferro Trio
creators.bio: Pianist Cass Ferro, bassist Del Okafor and drummer Mina Sato. Late sets, low lights, songs that take their time getting where they are going.

creators.name: Halden
creators.bio: One person, one four-track tape machine and a lake that freezes for five months a year. Music for long drives and early mornings.

creators.name: The Long Way Round
creators.bio: Two old friends take the scenic route through the small questions of modern life: attention, habits, wonder, and why we do the things we do.

creators.name: Liner Notes
creators.bio: Desmond Hale talks with the people whose names you only find in the small print: session players, engineers, arrangers and the stories behind the records.

creators.name: Small Machines
creators.bio: Imani Brooks visits the workshops of people who build, fix and care for the objects we live with, and asks what those objects have to teach us.

creators.name: Kitchen Table Economics
creators.bio: Two economists without the jargon. Nadia and Sam take one everyday transaction each week and follow the money until it stops.

creators.name: Odessa Wren
creators.bio: Sings over drum machines she rewires herself. Her second record was cut live in one night at a church hall on the east side.

creators.name: The Velvet Hours
creators.bio: A seven-piece with a horn section and a habit of recording to tape in a converted laundromat.

creators.name: Nadia Okoro Quartet
creators.bio: Saxophone, harp, upright bass and drums. Long pieces that take their time and earn it.

creators.name: Eli Marchetti
creators.bio: Solo piano, mostly standards, played like he is figuring them out for the first time.

creators.name: Lumen Field
creators.bio: Field recordings and modular synths. Every record is built from one place: a lake, a station, a forest at dawn.

creators.name: Wren & Hollow
creators.bio: Two voices and a borrowed banjo, writing about the coast and the people who stay.

creators.name: Kwame Asante Band
creators.bio: Twelve players, two drummers, one very long groove. A legendary live band finally on record.

creators.name: Sora Lake
creators.bio: Reverb-soaked guitar pop recorded in a cold apartment in Mile End.

creators.name: The Studio Floor
creators.bio: Producers and engineers on how one record got made, from the first demo to the final master.
works: The Drum Sound on Slow Honey

creators.name: Slow Cities
creators.bio: How streets, stoops and corner shops shape the way we live together.

songs.title: Paper Moons
songs.blurb: Unhurried neo-soul built on a secondhand Rhodes, brushed drums and a bassline that never raises its voice.

songs.title: Coastline Static
songs.blurb: Interlocking fingerpicked guitars and upright bass, recorded with the harbor windows open.

songs.title: Cathedral Lights
songs.blurb: Glowing analog arpeggios and a slow-motion drum machine. A choir kid's idea of a dance record.

songs.title: Harmattan Sun
songs.release: From the EP Gulf Coast Highlife
songs.blurb: Bright, circling guitar lines over a rolling percussion section. Impossible to hear sitting still.

songs.title: Slow Burn Avenue
songs.blurb: A late-set piano trio tune that takes its time, swinging gently under low lights.

songs.title: Glass Horizon
songs.blurb: Tape-warped pads and a soft, patient beat. Music for the hour before anyone else is awake.

episodes.title: In Defense of Boredom
episodes.topic: Theo spent a week without headphones. What he heard instead changed how he thinks about attention, and about why the best ideas arrive when nothing is happening.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Theo, I want to start with a confession from you.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Last week you sent me a text at eleven forty at night that just said, I can hear the refrigerator.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: That was the whole text.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: In my defense, it was a very loud refrigerator.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: It was not a loud refrigerator.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: You had just never noticed it before.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: That is true.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: That is, in a way, the entire episode.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Welcome to The Long Way Round.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I'm Priya Raman.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I'm Theo Marsh.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And this week, we are making the case for something that almost everyone is trying very hard to get rid of.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Boredom.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Boredom.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The empty minute.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The waiting room.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The walk to the train with nothing in your ears.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: So set it up for people.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: How did this start?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It started with a number, which is always a bad sign.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: My phone sends me that little weekly report, the screen time thing, and I usually swipe it away like a parking ticket.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: But a few weeks ago I actually looked at it, and the thing that jumped out wasn't the total.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It was a smaller number.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It was the number of times I picked up the phone before nine in the morning.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: How many?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I'm not going to say it out loud, because my mother listens to this show.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: But it was more times than I had been awake for hours.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Let's put it that way.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Okay.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And what bothered me was that I couldn't remember a single one of those pickups.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Not one.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: They weren't decisions.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: They were reflexes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Something like, there's a gap, fill the gap.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And the gap filler of choice for you is not even the phone screen, really.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: It's headphones.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It's headphones.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I am a headphones person.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Podcasts, music, audiobooks, anything.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: If I'm walking, cooking, doing the dishes, waiting for a kettle, there's something in my ears.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I always told myself that was a good thing.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I'm learning, I'm listening to good music, I'm not doom scrolling.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: This is the healthy version.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The virtuous version.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The virtuous version.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: So I decided to run a small, slightly ridiculous experiment.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: One week.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: No headphones.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: No audio at all while walking, commuting, cooking or cleaning.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: If I wanted to listen to something, I had to sit down and listen to it on purpose, and do nothing else.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Which, for the record, I told him was going to be miserable.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And you were right for about three days.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Okay, so walk me through it.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Day one.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: What actually happened?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Day one was genuinely uncomfortable.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I walked to the train and I kept reaching for my pocket, the way you reach for a light switch in a house you've moved out of.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: My hand knew the routine better than I did.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And the walk felt incredibly long.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It's eleven minutes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It felt like forty.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Because there was nothing to measure it against.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Normally the walk is measured in songs, or in half a podcast segment.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Without that, time just sort of sat there.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And my brain, for the first day or so, did not fill it with brilliant thoughts.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It filled it with nonsense.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Did I reply to that email.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: What's the thing I'm forgetting.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Why does that dog look like my uncle.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Which dog?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: There is a specific dog on Hawthorne Street.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: You would agree with me.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I'll trust you.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And the strangest part of those first two days was realizing how often I'd been using sound as a kind of shield.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Waiting in line at the pharmacy, there were five of us, and four of us had headphones in.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Nobody looked at anyone.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And without mine, I felt almost exposed, like I'd shown up to a party in pajamas.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I know that feeling exactly.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I get it in elevators.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: If I don't have something in my ears, I suddenly have no idea where to put my eyes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The headphones were doing a social job, not just an entertainment job.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: They were a little sign that said, don't talk to me, I'm busy.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I had been holding that sign up almost every waking hour without realizing it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: So days one and two were just noise.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: A kind of mental static.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And honestly, if the experiment had been two days long, I would have come back on this show and said, boredom is overrated, put your headphones back in.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: What changed?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Somewhere around day three, the static started to settle.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I can only describe it like this.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It was as if I had been standing next to a very loud machine for years, and someone switched it off, and for a while all I could hear was the ringing in my ears.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And then the ringing faded, and I started to hear the room.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The refrigerator.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The refrigerator, yes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: But also, I started noticing things on the walk.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: There's a man who runs a shoe repair shop near the station, and every morning at the same time he sweeps the sidewalk in front of his store, and then he sweeps a little bit of the sidewalk in front of the store next door, which is empty.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It's been empty for a year.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And he sweeps it anyway.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Oh, that's lovely.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I must have walked past him two hundred times.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I had never seen it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And then on day four, something happened that I did not expect, which is that I started having ideas again.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Real ones.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Not to-do list items.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Actual ideas.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I solved a problem at work in the shower that I'd been stuck on for two weeks.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I figured out what I wanted to say to my sister about something that had been bothering both of us.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I thought of three episode ideas for this show, two of which are bad.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: We'll see about that.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And the thing that struck me was that none of those ideas came while I was trying to think.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: They came in the gaps.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: On the walk, at the sink, waiting for the pasta water.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The exact moments I had been so carefully filling.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: So the gaps weren't empty.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: That's the thing I keep coming back to.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I thought I was wasting those minutes, and so I filled them with something valuable.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: But they were already being used.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: My brain was using them to connect things, to file things away, to notice.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I just never let it finish.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: There's actually a decent amount of research that lines up with what you're describing.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: When you're not focused on a task, there are networks in the brain that become more active, and they seem to be involved in exactly the kind of thing you're talking about.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Remembering, imagining, connecting your own experiences together.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: It's sometimes described as the brain's default mode.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The default mode.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I like that, because it suggests that this is the thing the brain wants to do when you leave it alone.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It's not idle.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It's doing its own work.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And we have essentially designed a world where it never gets left alone.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Do you know what it reminded me of?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: When I was a kid, on long car trips, there was always that stretch of highway where the radio station faded out and the next one hadn't come in yet.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And my dad would just leave it off for a while.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Nobody talked.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: We just watched the fields go by.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I remember those stretches better than almost anything we actually listened to.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The silence between stations.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The silence between stations.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It used to be built into life.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: You couldn't avoid it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Now you have to go looking for it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I'm not anti-technology.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I make a podcast, I love audio more than almost anything.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: But I think I had stopped choosing what I listened to.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I was just pouring sound into every container I could find.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And when I took it away, the thing I missed most wasn't the content.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It was the habit of never being alone with my own head.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: So by the end of the week, did you want your headphones back?

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I wanted some of them back.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And that was the real discovery.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: When the week ended, I didn't go back to wall-to-wall audio.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I started choosing.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I'd sit down with an album, the whole album, start to finish, and actually listen to it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I'd pick one episode of something and give it my full attention.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And everything I listened to on purpose felt better.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Richer.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Like the difference between eating standing over the sink and sitting down for a meal.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Less listening, but better listening.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Less listening, better listening, and a lot more noticing.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I want to push back a little, though, because I think there's a version of this conversation that turns into a lecture.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Put your phone down, go for a walk, look at a tree.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Look at a tree, Priya.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And I don't think people are filling every gap because they're foolish.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I think a lot of people are tired.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: They're lonely.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The gaps can be uncomfortable for real reasons.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Sometimes the thing waiting in the quiet is something you don't want to think about.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: That's completely fair.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And I'll be honest, part of the discomfort in those first few days was exactly that.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Things I had been putting off thinking about came up.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And there's a reason I'd been keeping the volume up.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: So what do you say to someone who hears this and thinks, that sounds nice for you, but my quiet isn't relaxing.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I'd say you don't have to do a whole week.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Start with one container.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: One walk, one commute, one load of dishes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Leave one gap open on purpose and see what wanders into it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It doesn't have to be profound.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: It might just be the dog on Hawthorne Street.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I think there's something about choosing in there too.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: You said that once you stopped filling everything automatically, you started choosing what to listen to.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And that feels like the bigger idea.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Yes.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Boredom is not the goal.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The goal is to be the one making the choice.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Boredom is just what you have to walk through to get your choices back.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I like that a lot.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Boredom as a kind of hallway.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: A hallway with a very loud refrigerator in it.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Can I make this slightly bigger than one person's habits, though?

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Because I don't think the gaps disappeared by accident.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: No, they didn't.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: A lot of what we use every day is built to fill them.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The next video starts before you've decided you want it.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The feed has no bottom.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The episode ends and another one is already counting down.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Those are design decisions.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Somebody chose to remove the moment where you would have had to choose.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: The pause where you might have stopped.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And I don't think the people who build those things are villains.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Most of them are trying to make something people enjoy.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: But if your only measure of success is how much time people spend with you, then every gap looks like a leak.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And you plug it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Which is interesting, because the best experiences I had during that week were the opposite.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: They were the ones that ended.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: An album has a last song.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: A good conversation has a natural end.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: You get to the end and you feel full, not drained.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: I'd love to see more things designed around that feeling.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Around being satisfied, rather than being held.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Something that helps you find what you'd love, gives it to you, and then lets you go.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Respecting the gap.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Respecting the gap.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Imagine if that was a feature.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: You finished the thing you came for.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Go outside.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I would pay for that app.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I would pay real money.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: You would pay for an app that tells you to stop using it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: I would pay for an app that knows when I'm done.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: That's different.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Okay, before we go, I want to give people a tiny assignment, because we always do this and people seem to actually like it.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Homework.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Everyone's favorite.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: This week, pick one gap.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Just one.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: A walk, a commute, a wait.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Leave it empty.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: Don't fill it with anything.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: And then write to us and tell us what you noticed.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And if what you noticed is a dog that looks like a relative, we especially want to hear about it.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: That's our show.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: The Long Way Round is made by me, Priya Raman.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: And me, Theo Marsh.

cues.speaker: THEO
cues.text: Thanks for taking the long way with us.

cues.speaker: PRIYA
cues.text: See you next week.

cues.text: This is Liner Notes.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I'm Desmond Hale.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Every record you love has a list of names printed in very small type somewhere on the sleeve, and on this show we go looking for the people behind those names.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: My guest today has played bass on, by her own estimate, somewhere north of four hundred recordings.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Pop records, country records, film scores, a few jingles she would prefer we not mention.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Please don't mention the jingles.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I won't mention the jingles.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Rosa Quintero, welcome to Liner Notes.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Thank you, Desmond.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It's strange to be on this side of a microphone.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Usually when I'm in a room like this, I'm the one in the corner trying not to make any noise between takes.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Let's start at the beginning.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: How does someone become a session bassist?

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Because I don't think most people know that's even a job.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Most people don't.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And honestly, when I was young, I didn't either.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I grew up in San Antonio, and my uncle played bass in a conjunto band, and I used to sit under the table at family parties and watch his right hand.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Not his face, not the singer, his right hand.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: There was something about how little he moved.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Everyone else was dancing and sweating and he was just standing there, completely calm, holding the whole thing together.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: The quiet center of the room.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I think I decided pretty early that I wanted to be that person.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I didn't want to be the one out front.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I wanted to be the one everybody was leaning on without realizing it.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: And how did that turn into a career?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Slowly, and then all at once.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I played in bar bands for years.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I taught lessons.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I played in pit orchestras for musicals, which is the best training in the world, because you have to read anything they put in front of you and you can never, ever be late.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And then a producer I'd done a few demos for called me on a Tuesday afternoon and said, our bass player is sick, can you be here in an hour.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I went.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And that was the first real session.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: What do you remember about that first day?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Terror.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Pure terror.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And the coffee.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The coffee was very good.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Studios always have very good coffee, because they know everyone is terrified.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I want to talk about what the job actually is, because I think there's a misunderstanding that a session player is just someone who plays what's written.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Sometimes it is.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Sometimes there's a full chart and they want exactly that, and your job is to play it perfectly, with great feel, on the first or second take.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But a lot of the time, especially in pop and rock, there's no chart.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: There's a demo.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Maybe it's the songwriter singing over an acoustic guitar on their phone.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And the producer says, give us something.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Give us something.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Give us something.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Which is the most terrifying and the most wonderful sentence in the business.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Because now you're not just playing.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You're writing.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You're deciding what this song sounds like underneath.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And the trick, the thing that took me years to understand, is that the best part is almost never the most impressive one.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Say more about that.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Young players, and I was one, want to show you what they can do.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They want to fill every space.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But the song doesn't need you to be impressive.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The song needs you to make the singer sound like the most important person in the world.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: So most of what I do, honestly, is decide what not to play.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Which brings us to the story I asked you here to tell.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: There's one bassline in particular that has followed you around for a long time.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It has.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It really has.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And the funny thing is, it was never supposed to exist.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Tell me about the day.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: So this was a long time ago.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I was booked for a three-hour session on a single for a singer who was, at that point, not well known.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Nobody in the room thought this song was the big one.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It was a filler date.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The producer was tired, the drummer had a flight to catch, and we had been working on this one song for most of the afternoon, and it just wasn't sitting right.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The verses felt stiff.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Everyone was playing correctly, and it was completely dead.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: That happens.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It happens all the time.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: So the producer calls a break, and everyone goes to get coffee, and I stayed in the room because I was frustrated and I wanted to figure it out.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I started just playing around.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Not the part.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Just noodling.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I took the root notes I'd been playing, which were very straight, very on the beat, and I started leaving out the first note of every bar.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Leaving it out.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Leaving it out.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Just letting the drum take the downbeat alone, and then coming in a little late, a little behind, almost like the bass was answering the kick drum instead of agreeing with it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And then I added this little climb at the end of every second bar, three notes, nothing fancy.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I was just playing it for myself.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I didn't think anyone was listening.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: But somebody was.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The engineer.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The engineer had never stopped recording.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: This was something engineers do, by the way, the good ones.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They just leave the tape running because they know people do their best playing when they think it doesn't count.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: So the producer comes back with his coffee, and the engineer says, you need to hear this.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And he plays back me noodling, completely alone, no drums, no singer, just this lopsided little bass figure.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: And what did the producer say?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: He didn't say anything for a while.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: He just listened to it twice.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And then he said, that's the song.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Build everything around that.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And they literally did.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The drummer missed his flight.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: We stayed another three hours.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They rearranged the whole track so that everything was leaning on this part I'd invented by accident while everyone else was getting coffee.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I remember the singer coming in that evening, after we'd rebuilt the track.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: She hadn't been there for any of it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: She put on the headphones, and they played her the new version, and she just started laughing.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Not because it was funny.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Because suddenly she knew how to sing it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The verse that had been stiff all day, she sang in one take.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: She said, oh, it's a sway.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I thought it was a march, but it's a sway.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: The bass told her how to sing it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The bass told her how to sing it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: That's the thing people don't understand about the low end.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You don't really hear it consciously, most of the time.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But your body hears it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It tells you whether to stand still or lean, whether to rush or relax.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Change the bass, and you change what the singer's body thinks the song is about.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: And the record?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The record did very well.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Much better than anyone expected.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And for years afterward, I would be in a grocery store, or in a taxi, or at a wedding, and I would hear that bassline.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Just that little lopsided thing, coming out of a speaker.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: People would be humming it in line at the bank.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And nobody had any idea that it was me.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: My name was on the sleeve, in that very small type you mentioned, but nobody reads that.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The first time I heard it on the radio, I was in a cab in the rain, and the driver had it on, and I made him turn it up.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And he looked at me in the mirror like I was crazy, because I was sitting in the back seat with my eyes closed, playing air bass on my knee.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Did you tell him?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I did.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I said, that's me, on the bass.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And he said, sure it is.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And turned it back down.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: How did that feel?

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Hearing it everywhere and being invisible?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I've thought about this a lot.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I think at the time, honestly, it felt wonderful.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It felt like I had a secret.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I'd be at a party and someone would put the song on and everyone would start dancing, and I'd think, you're dancing to something I did with my hands in an empty room.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It felt like magic.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: And now?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Now it's more complicated.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Because over the years I watched the business change, and the small type got smaller, and then on a lot of streaming services, it disappeared entirely.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You can listen to a song a thousand times and have no way of knowing who played on it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And that's not just about credit for me.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It's that the listener loses something too.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: If you love that bassline, you might love the other four hundred things I've played on.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But there's no road from the song back to me.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: No road back to the person.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: No road back to the person.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And I think that's what we've lost.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Not the money, although, yes, also the money.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It's the connection.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The ability for someone who loves a sound to go and find where it came from.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I want to stay on that, because it's something we talk about a lot on this show.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: When you were growing up, how did you find the players you loved?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Liner notes.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Exactly like the name of your show.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I would buy a record, and I would read every word on the back.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Who played bass, who engineered it, which studio.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And then I'd go to the record store and look for other albums with the same names on them.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: That's how I found half the musicians I've ever loved.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It was like following a trail of breadcrumbs.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: And that trail is harder to follow now.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It's harder.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: It's not impossible.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: There are people working on it, there are databases, some services are getting better about showing credits.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But it's not the default.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The default is a song title and an artist name, and everyone else is invisible.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: What would you want listeners to do differently?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Be curious.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: That's all.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: When something moves you, ask who made it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Not just the singer.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Ask who played the drums.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Ask who wrote the string arrangement.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Ask who engineered it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Because those people are out there, and they're making other things, and you might love those things too.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: You said earlier that most of your job is deciding what not to play.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I want to come back to that, because I think it's true of a lot more than bass.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I think it's true of almost everything.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: When I teach young players now, the first exercise I give them is to play a song with half the notes.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Take whatever part they've worked out, and cut it in half.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And they hate it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They feel naked.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And then they listen back, and it sounds twice as good.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Why does that work?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Because silence is an instrument.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: When you leave a space, the listener leans in.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They fill it with their own anticipation.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: If you play every beat, nobody's leaning in.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: They're just being told.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: There's something about trust in that.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Yes.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You're trusting the listener to meet you halfway.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And honestly, I think a lot of music now is afraid of that.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Every second is full, because everyone's worried that if there's a gap, someone will skip.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: So you end up with records that never breathe.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Do you think listeners actually want the space?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I think listeners want to feel something.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And it's very hard to feel something when you're never given room to.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: The records I love most, the ones I've played a thousand times, all have air in them.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You can hear the room.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You can hear somebody decide not to play.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: You can hear somebody decide not to play.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: That might be my favorite sentence anyone has said on this show.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: You can have it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: No charge.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Rosa, before we go, what are you working on now?

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I'm actually making my own record, for the first time, at the age of fifty-two.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: All bass, all instrumental, recorded in my living room.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: I don't know if anyone will listen to it.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: But I wanted to know what it would sound like if I played everything I've spent thirty years leaving out.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I can't wait to hear it.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Rosa Quintero, thank you for coming to Liner Notes.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: Thank you, Desmond.

cues.speaker: ROSA
cues.text: And thank you to every engineer who ever forgot to stop recording.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: This has been Liner Notes.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: I'm Desmond Hale.

cues.speaker: DESMOND
cues.text: Read the small type.

episodes.title: What an Old Radio Knows
episodes.topic: Walter Fenn has restored tube radios for forty years. Imani asks him how a radio actually finds a station, and what tuning in has to do with paying attention.

highlight.title: How a radio finds a voice in the noise

chapters.title: How a radio finds a voice in the noise

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: This is Small Machines.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: I'm Imani Brooks.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Today I'm in a workshop on the second floor of an old textile building, and every surface in this room is covered with radios.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Wooden radios, plastic radios, radios the size of a suitcase, radios the size of a sandwich.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Some of them have their backs off and their insides spread out on the bench like a patient on an operating table.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: And sitting across from me is the man who has been bringing them back to life for forty years.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Walter Fenn, thank you for having me.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Thank you for climbing the stairs.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Most people complain about the stairs.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: The stairs were a lot.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The stairs keep out the people who aren't serious.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: How did you start doing this?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: My father had a radio in the kitchen.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: A big walnut tabletop set.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And when I was about eleven, it stopped working, and he was going to throw it out.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I asked if I could have it instead.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I didn't know anything.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I took the back off and just stared at it.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: All these glass tubes and little colored components and wires going everywhere.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I remember thinking, somewhere in here is the voice of the ballgame announcer, and I'm going to find it.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Did you find it?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It took me most of a year.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I went to the library, I read everything I could find, I bothered every television repairman in town.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And one day I replaced a little part, a capacitor, that cost about a quarter, and I plugged it in, and I waited for the tubes to warm up, which takes a while, and then out of the speaker came this crackle, and then a voice.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I was hooked for life.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: How many radios do you think you've restored since then?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I stopped counting at three thousand.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That was a long time ago.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: I want to ask you something that I suspect a lot of people have never really understood, and I'll include myself.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: When you turn the dial on a radio, what is actually happening?

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: How does it find a station?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That's my favorite question.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Nobody asks me that anymore.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Alright.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: So the first thing to understand is that right now, in this room, the air is full of voices.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Every station within a hundred miles is broadcasting at the same time.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Music, news, ballgames, preachers, weather reports, all of it, passing through this room, passing through you and me, right this second.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: That's a slightly unsettling thought.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It's a beautiful thought.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: But it's also a problem.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Because if you just caught all of it at once, you'd hear nothing but noise.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: A roar.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: So the whole job of a radio, really the entire purpose of the machine, is to ignore almost everything, and let in just one thing.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: So a radio is a machine for ignoring.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That's exactly right.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I've never heard anyone put it that way, but that's exactly right.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Each station broadcasts on its own frequency, its own rate of vibration.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And inside the radio there's a circuit, a coil and a capacitor working together, that naturally wants to vibrate at one particular rate.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: When you turn the dial, you're changing that capacitor, which changes the rate the circuit prefers.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And when the circuit's preference lines up with a station's frequency, that station's signal suddenly gets very strong inside the radio, and everything else stays weak.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Like pushing a child on a swing.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Very much like that.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: If you push at the right moment, every time, the swing goes higher and higher.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Push at the wrong moments and it barely moves.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The station is pushing at its own rhythm.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The tuning circuit only swings for the one that matches.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: And then?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And then there's a very clever trick, which is the reason these old radios work as well as they do.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Instead of trying to amplify every station at its own frequency, which is hard, the radio converts whatever station you've chosen down to one fixed frequency inside the set.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Always the same one.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And then it has a series of stages that are built to amplify that one frequency extremely well, and nothing else.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It's called a superheterodyne, which is a terrible word for a wonderful idea.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Why is it wonderful?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Because it means the radio doesn't have to be good at everything.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It only has to be very, very good at one thing, and then it translates the whole world into that one thing.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: When I explain it to young people, I say, it's like having a friend who speaks every language, and no matter who's talking, your friend translates it into the one language you understand perfectly.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: And what about the static?

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: The hiss you hear between stations.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Where does that come from?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Some of it is the radio itself.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Every warm thing makes a little bit of noise, even the parts inside the set, just from the atoms moving around.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: But a lot of it is the universe.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Lightning storms on the other side of the country.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Electrical motors down the street.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And a small part of it, a very small part, is left over from the beginning of everything.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Energy that's been travelling across space for a very long time, and ends up as a tiny bit of hiss in your kitchen.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: So between stations, I'm listening to the universe.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Between stations, you're listening to everything that isn't trying to talk to you.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And when you land on a station, all of that falls away, and one person comes through clear.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I've been doing this for forty years and that moment still gets me.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Every single time.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Noise, noise, noise, and then, a voice.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: I love that.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: And it makes me think about why these machines matter to you beyond the engineering.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Well.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I'll tell you something I don't usually say on a recording.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I think I've spent my whole life around machines that are very good at paying attention.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That's what a radio is.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It sits in a room full of noise, and it chooses one voice, and it gives that voice its complete attention, and it makes it clear enough for a person to hear.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And over the years I've come to think that's most of what a good life is, too.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The world is full of noise.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Everybody is broadcasting at once.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And the work, the real work, is tuning in to the thing that deserves your attention, and giving it all of yourself.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Tuning in.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Tuning in.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: My wife used to say I listened to radios better than I listened to people.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: She was not wrong.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I've been trying to get better at that.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Let's talk about the people who bring these radios to you.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Who are they?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Oh, everyone.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Collectors, sometimes.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: But mostly it's families.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Somebody's grandmother passed, and in the attic there's the radio she listened to every morning while she made breakfast.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And they don't care if it's valuable.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: They want to hear it play again.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: They want to hear the sound she heard.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: That must be an emotional moment.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It's the best part of the job.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: When they come to pick it up, I always make them wait while it warms up.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I don't let them just take it home.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I turn it on, and we stand here together in the shop, and there's that hum, and then a crackle, and then a voice comes through.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I've seen grown men cry at a weather report.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: What do you think people are really responding to in that moment?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Presence.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: A radio is a live thing.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: When you turn it on, somebody, somewhere, is talking right now.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Not recorded for you, not chosen by a computer for you.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Live.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: There's a person on the other end of that sound.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I think people miss that feeling, of being one of a lot of people listening to the same thing at the same time, without being able to see each other.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Can you show me what you're working on right now?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Sure.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: This one here, the cream colored one with the gold dial.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Came in last week.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Belonged to a woman who ran a diner for thirty years, and this sat on the counter by the register the whole time.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Her son brought it in.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: You can see the finish is worn right here, on the top, in the shape of a hand.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That's where she rested her hand every time she reached for the cash drawer.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Oh, wow.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: You can actually see it.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Thirty years of the same gesture.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I won't refinish that part.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: People always ask me to make things look new.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: And I'll fix anything that's broken, but I try very hard not to erase anything that's true.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That handprint is the most valuable thing on the radio.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: What's wrong with it, mechanically?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Mostly the usual.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Old capacitors that have dried out, a tube that's tired, a dial cord that snapped.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The dial cord is the little string that connects the knob to the needle, so when you turn the knob, the needle slides across the numbers.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: When that string breaks, the radio might still work perfectly, but you can't see where you are.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: You're tuning blind.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: That feels like a metaphor.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Everything in here is a metaphor if you stay long enough.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: That's the danger of this job.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: You start thinking every radio is about life.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Is that so bad?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: No.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I suppose it isn't.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: It's kept me company.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Walter, what happens to all of this when you retire?

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: I'm training two apprentices.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: One is a nineteen year old who found me through a video online, which I find very funny.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The other is a retired schoolteacher who says she's always wanted to know how things work.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: They're both better at soldering than I was at their age.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: The radios will be fine.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Walter Fenn, thank you for letting me into the shop.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Thank you for asking how a radio works.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Come back anytime.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Bring your own coffee.

cues.speaker: WALTER
cues.text: Mine is terrible.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: This has been Small Machines.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: I'm Imani Brooks.

cues.speaker: IMANI
cues.text: Take care of your things, and they'll take care of you.

episodes.title: Who Gets Paid When You Press Play?
episodes.topic: Nadia and Sam follow a single stream of a single song from your headphones back to the people who made it, and ask what a healthy middle class for musicians would look like.

highlight.title: Following one stream back to the artist

chapters.title: Following one stream back to the artist
What a healthier system might look like

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Nadia, I want you to do something for me.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Take out your phone, open any music app, and play a song.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Any song.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Okay.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Done.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Congratulations.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: You have just set in motion one of the most complicated payment systems in the modern economy.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: I just wanted to hear a song, Sam.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: I know.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's what makes it beautiful.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Welcome to Kitchen Table Economics.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: I'm Nadia Kessler.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And I'm Sam Okafor.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Every week we take one ordinary thing you do, and we follow the money until it stops.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And this week, the ordinary thing is pressing play.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: So why this one?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Why now?

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Because I keep having the same conversation at parties.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Somebody finds out I'm an economist, and they say, okay, settle this.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Is it true that musicians make basically nothing from streaming?

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And I always give a mushy answer, because the honest answer is, it depends, and it's complicated.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And I wanted to actually sit down and trace it, step by step, so that next time I can give a less mushy answer.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And to be clear, we are going to keep this general.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The exact numbers vary a lot by service, by country, by contract, and they change over time.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: So we're not going to pretend there's one official rate.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: We're going to follow the shape of the money.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: The shape of the money.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's a good name for a band.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's a terrible name for a band.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Okay.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So let's actually do it.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: You pressed play.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Where does the money start?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It starts with you, the listener, and it starts before you pressed anything.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It starts when you paid your monthly subscription, or, if you're on a free tier, when an advertiser paid to put an ad in front of you.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's the pool.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: All the subscription money and all the ad money for a given month, in a given market, goes into one very large pot.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: One big pot.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And here's the part that surprises people.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: In the most common model, your money doesn't follow your listening directly.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It goes into the pot with everyone else's.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The service takes its share off the top, to run the business.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And then the remaining money is divided up based on each rights holder's share of total streams that month.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: So if one artist's songs were one percent of all the streams on the service, the people who own those recordings get roughly one percent of the pot set aside for music.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Which means that if you only listen to a small jazz trio all month, but most people are listening to the biggest pop stars in the world, a lot of your subscription is effectively going to the pop stars.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Effectively, yes.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Your listening is a vote, but it's one vote in a giant election.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's what people call the pro rata model.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And there's a real debate about an alternative, sometimes called user centric, where your money would follow only the artists you actually played.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Some services have experimented with versions of it.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's not a magic fix, but it changes who wins.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Okay, so the pot has been split.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Now the money is heading out the door.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Where does it go next?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: This is where it splits again.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Because a song is actually two different things legally.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: There's the recording, the actual audio, the performance.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And then there's the composition, the melody and the lyrics, the song as written.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Those usually have different owners.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So two streams of money for one stream of music.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The recording money usually goes to whoever owns the master, which is often a record label, or a distributor if the artist is independent.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And then the artist gets their share according to their contract.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: For a traditional label deal, that share might be a minority of what comes in.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: For an independent artist using a distributor, they might keep most of it, but they're also paying for everything themselves.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And the composition side?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The composition side flows through publishers and collecting societies, and eventually to the songwriters.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Which might be the same person as the artist, or might be three other people in a room in Nashville.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So if we imagine one single play, by the time it reaches the person who actually made the music, it has been divided, and divided, and divided again.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Divided by the service, divided by the market share of the whole pot, divided between recording and composition, divided by label or distributor, divided by contract, and divided among co-writers.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And each of those divisions has a perfectly good reason behind it.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's just that when you stack them all up, the amount reaching any one person from a single play is a tiny fraction of a cent.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Which is why the honest answer to the party question is, it's not that the system pays nothing.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It's that it's designed to pay well at enormous scale.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: If you have hundreds of millions of plays, it can add up to a real living.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: If you have ten thousand, it's a nice dinner.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And the uncomfortable part is the middle.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The artist with a real, dedicated audience, people who love their work, who listen every week, but who will never be in the top one percent of global streams.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That artist is the one the math is hardest on.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And I want to be fair here, because it's easy to make this sound like a villain story.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It mostly isn't.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The services are running on margins that aren't as huge as people assume.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Labels fund a lot of recordings that never earn back their costs.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Publishers chase down money that would otherwise go uncollected.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Every hand in the chain is doing real work.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It's not a heist.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It's a funnel.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's a funnel.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: A very wide top, a lot of layers, and a narrow spout at the bottom where the artist is standing with a cup.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's a bleak image.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: You asked me to follow the money.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: The musical middle class.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The musical middle class.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And that's what I actually care about.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Not whether superstars are rich.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: They'll be fine.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Whether someone with fifty thousand devoted listeners can make a living doing this.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So let's talk about that.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: If you could redesign this, what would you change?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: I'd start with discovery, honestly, before payment.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Because the money follows attention, and attention right now is incredibly concentrated.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Most listening goes to a relatively small slice of artists, and a lot of that is driven by what gets surfaced to people.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: If you help listeners actually find the artists they'd love, and not just the ones everyone else is already playing, the money starts to spread out on its own.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So the problem isn't only how you split the pie.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It's who gets invited to the table in the first place.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And the second thing is direct connection.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: The artists who seem to be doing best in the middle are the ones who have a real relationship with their listeners.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: People who come to the shows, buy the vinyl, support them directly.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Streaming is often the front door.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's how people find you.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: But the living gets made in the relationship that comes after.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's interesting, because it reframes streaming as less of a cash register and more of a radio station.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's actually a great way to put it.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: For decades, radio didn't pay artists much directly either, in a lot of cases.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: But it introduced you to them.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And then you went and bought the record.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: So the question becomes, what's the modern version of hearing something on the radio, falling in love, and going to find the person who made it?

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And how do we make that path as short as possible.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Can we talk about the listener for a second?

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Because I think listeners get either blamed or ignored in this conversation, and neither is fair.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Agreed.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Most people are not choosing to underpay musicians.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: They're choosing a convenient way to hear music, at a price that feels reasonable.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's a completely rational decision.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And honestly, the convenience is incredible.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: When I was a teenager I had about forty albums, and I knew every one of them by heart, because that was all I had.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Now I have basically every recording ever made in my pocket.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And how many of them do you actually listen to?

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's the uncomfortable question.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Because when I look at my history, I mostly listen to the same few hundred songs, over and over.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Infinite choice, and I keep choosing the same thing.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's very normal.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: When everything is available, the hard part isn't access.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: It's discovery.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Finding the thing you didn't know you were looking for.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And that's where I think there's real value still to be created, for listeners and artists at the same time.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: The economist in me wants to point out that the scarce resource has changed.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: It used to be music.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Now it's attention.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: And whoever helps people spend their attention well, in a way that feels good rather than exhausting, is solving the actual problem.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And if that also happens to send listeners toward artists in the middle, the people with real audiences who just haven't been found yet...

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Then you've helped the listener and the artist with the same move.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's the rare thing in economics.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: A trade where both sides actually come out ahead.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Okay, homework time.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: This week, pick one artist you love who you're pretty sure is not famous.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And do one thing that sends money to them more directly than a stream.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Buy a record, buy a ticket, buy a shirt.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Or just tell a friend.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Attention is also currency.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Attention is also currency.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: That's going on the whiteboard.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: Everything goes on the whiteboard.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: That's our show.

cues.speaker: NADIA
cues.text: I'm Nadia Kessler.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: And I'm Sam Okafor.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: This has been Kitchen Table Economics.

cues.speaker: SAM
cues.text: Follow the money.

hh-juniper-2am.text: The Rhodes at 2am is a genre of its own. Please keep the tape hiss.
Already know this one is going to wreck me.

Would happily listen to forty minutes of this exact loop.
Del says thank you. I say we'll see.

Already recording it. Valves arrive Thursday.

hh-teodora-soundcheck.text: See you in that enormous room tonight, front left.
The reverb in there is doing half the work. Gorgeous.
front left gets the encore wave.

hh-priya-walk.text: Thinking-out-loud walks are my favourite part of this show. More of these.
These voice notes are better than most finished podcasts.

splitting it 50/50 with the wind, yes.

Put this on for focus and forgot to work.

hh-juniper-lyrics.text: The coffee ring is the best part of the lyric sheet.
Crossed-out line in verse two is a whole other song.
